documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

48 y/o man joining the practice. Supervises a shift at a distribution warehouse; no regular exercise. Wanted a doctor who answers the phone.

Diabetes: type 2, found about four years ago at his previous office on routine labs. Metformin 1000 mg BID since then, tolerating it, occasional loose stool in the first year that settled. Last A1c he remembers was "in the sixes." No eye exam in over a year. No numbness in the feet, no polyuria.
Statin: atorvastatin 20 mg daily, started by the old office for the diabetes. No muscle aches.
Gout: one attack in the right big toe a few years back, treated short-term at the prior office, no recurrence that he can recall, never on a daily gout pill.
Kidney stone: one, roughly six years ago, passed it at home after a rough couple of days. No procedure.

Meds: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily.
Allergies: none to medications.
Surgeries: none.
FH: father with type 2 DM and gout. Mother with high blood pressure. Paternal uncle drank heavily.
SH: never smoked. Alcohol "socially, a few on weekends." No drug use. Married. Day shift, sometimes stays late.

ROS: negative in detail, including no chest pain, dyspnea, dysuria, flank pain, joint swelling.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet, BP normal today. Ht 180 cm, wt 103.8 kg, BMI about 32. Well-appearing, heavyset. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen protuberant, soft, nontender, no organomegaly. Feet: pulses 2+, monofilament intact bilaterally, no calluses or ulcers. No joint swelling or tophi. Skin clear.

Assessment/plan
1. Type 2 diabetes, on metformin. A1c, CMP, urine albumin/creatinine today. Eye exam referral to an optometrist. Continue metformin.
2. Lipids on atorvastatin 20. Lipid panel today.
3. Gout, remote single flare. No treatment needed now. Will check uric acid if he has symptoms.
4. History of kidney stone. Hydration discussed.
5. Weight: BMI 32. Talked briefly about activity; he'd rather tackle it later.
6. Prevention: Tdap given today. HCV and HIV screening today, he agreed. Colon cancer screening due at 45 under the newer guidance once he's eligible, will plan with him in the next year or two. Flu shot when it arrives.
7. Records requested from the prior office.

RTC 6 months for diabetes, sooner as needed.

ANNUAL PHYSICAL — 50 y/o M

No complaints today. Here for his yearly exam.

Diabetes: metformin 1000 mg BID, takes it reliably. Labs from Tuesday: fasting glucose 98, A1c 6.2. Well controlled.
Lipids on atorvastatin 20: total 190, HDL 40, LDL 120, TG 150.

Activity: mostly at a desk or walking the floor at the warehouse, drives in, no regular exercise. Diet heavy on takeout.
Alcohol: social, per pt. Never smoker.
FH reviewed: father T2DM and gout, mother hypertension, paternal uncle with alcohol problems.

Exam
BP 138/90 today, HR normal. In October it was 142/92. BMI 32, weight carried centrally. General: comfortable. HEENT normal. Neck no thyromegaly. CV regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen obese, soft, nontender. Ext no edema. Feet: sensation intact, pulses 2+. Skin normal. PHQ-2 0.

Assessment and plan
1. Essential hypertension: two elevated readings on separate days, diabetic. Start lisinopril 20 mg daily. BMP in 2 weeks (K, creatinine). Home cuff if he can get one.
2. T2DM: at goal, continue metformin.
3. Lipids: continue atorvastatin 20.
4. Weight/central obesity: we set concrete goals together — walking 30 minutes 5 days a week, swapping soda and takeout lunches, aiming for 5% weight loss over 6 months. Recheck in 3 months.
5. Shingrix #1 today, #2 in 2 to 6 months.
6. Colonoscopy 2021 normal. Eye exam 12/2021 no retinopathy.

RTC 3 months.

Annual physical.

New issue: since around the holidays food has been "getting stuck" partway down when he swallows. Points to the middle of his chest. Worse with bread and meat, has had to stop and drink water to get things down. Sometimes liquids too. Brings some up undigested now and then. No pain with swallowing, no heartburn to speak of, no weight loss, no vomiting blood, no black stools. Never had this before.

Chronic: metformin, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 20. No changes. Alcohol: "a few on weekends." Never smoker.

Exam: vitals per flowsheet. Weight stable at about 104 kg. Oropharynx normal. Neck without masses or nodes. Heart and lungs normal. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Feet normal. PHQ-2 0.

A/P
1. Dysphagia, about 3 months, solids more than liquids, with regurgitation. Needs endoscopic evaluation. GI referral placed, asked for the earliest slot. Eat slowly, small bites, upright after meals. Call if he can't keep liquids down or loses weight.
2. T2DM, HTN, lipids: labs today, meds unchanged.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation and upper endoscopy
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION
Patient: Darren Upton   DOB: 07/10/1971   Date of visit: 06/05/2023
Referring: primary care physician

Reason for referral: difficulty swallowing.

History: 51-year-old man followed by his PCP for hypertension and elevated weight, also with type 2 diabetes. About six months of swallowing trouble that has steadily worsened, now with both solid food and liquids. Describes a sense of food hanging up behind the mid-sternum after he eats, and intermittent regurgitation of food that comes back up unchanged. He has not lost a meaningful amount of weight. No vomiting. Bowel habits unchanged.

Medications: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin. Allergies: NKDA.
Social: never smoker; alcohol per patient, social.

Exam: BP 138/86, HR 78. BMI 32. Comfortable. Heart regular, lungs clear. Abdomen soft without hepatosplenomegaly or masses.

Labs drawn today: hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, fasting glucose 152 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, TSH 2.5 uIU/mL, electrolytes normal.

UPPER ENDOSCOPY (same day, monitored anesthesia care):
Esophagus dilated, with retained food debris in the lumen despite fasting. No mass. No stricture. Mucosa otherwise unremarkable after lavage. The scope passed into the stomach with gentle pressure at the gastroesophageal junction. Stomach and duodenum normal.

Impression: dysphagia with a dilated, food-retaining esophagus and no obstructing lesion; a primary motility disorder is suspected.
Plan: high-resolution esophageal manometry, scheduled. Liquid-heavy diet the day before procedures. We will send results.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: High-resolution esophageal manometry
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
ESOPHAGEAL MANOMETRY REPORT
Patient: Darren Upton   Study date: 06/14/2023
Indication: dysphagia; dilated esophagus with retained food on endoscopy 06/05/2023.

Catheter placed transnasally without difficulty. Ten wet swallows analyzed.
Findings: aperistalsis of the esophageal body on all swallows. Incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter with elevated integrated relaxation pressure.
Interpretation: findings consistent with achalasia.

Plan from GI: treatment options reviewed with patient (pneumatic dilation versus surgical myotomy versus endoscopic myotomy). He prefers balloon dilation; being scheduled.
Gastroenterology

documents.title: Your GI results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Darren, I received the GI report yesterday. The swallowing study shows achalasia: the muscle at the bottom of the esophagus doesn't relax when you swallow and the esophagus itself isn't squeezing food down. That explains the food sticking. The scope showed no growth or narrowing, which is reassuring. The GI team says you chose the balloon stretching procedure. That's a good first-line option. Let me know when it's scheduled and how it goes.

documents.title: Had the balloon procedure
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Had the balloon stretch done last Wednesday the 9th. Sore throat for a day. Food is going down way better, I had a sandwich today with no problem. They said they'd send you something.

documents.title: RE: Had the balloon procedure
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That's great news. Haven't received their report yet, I'll keep an eye out. Any chest pain, fever, or trouble breathing in the days after a dilation should be checked right away. Glad you can eat a sandwich again.

OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY — ADDICTION SERVICES
Initial evaluation, date of service 11/30/2023
Patient: Darren Upton, 52 M. Referred by PCP.

Chief concern: wants to stop drinking.

History: Recently diagnosed with achalasia and treated with dilation; also followed for diabetes and hypertension (on metformin and lisinopril). Reports drinking six beers a day for about the last ten years. Several attempts to quit on his own, none sustained beyond a couple of weeks. Motivated now because drinking is straining his family life and he feels it is affecting his performance as a shift supervisor. Denies illicit drug use. Has never been prescribed opioids. No history of withdrawal seizures or delirium. No prior treatment.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Family: paternal uncle with alcohol use disorder.

Exam: BP 138/85, HR 78, BMI 30. Calm, cooperative, good eye contact, euthymic, linear thought process, no SI/HI, no perceptual disturbance. Insight and judgment fair to good. No tremor. Liver edge palpable about 2 cm below the right costal margin. No jaundice, no ascites, no spider angiomas.

Labs: CBC within normal limits. AST 45 U/L (mildly high), ALT 52 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 85 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

Assessment: Alcohol use disorder, moderate.

Plan:
- Referred to our intensive outpatient counseling program; intake information given.
- Discussed medication to reduce craving (naltrexone). He would like to try counseling first and revisit medication if he struggles.
- Gradual reduction discussed with return precautions for withdrawal symptoms.
- Follow-up with us as needed through the counseling program.

Psychiatry

Started folic acid 1 mg daily, sent to pharmacy. Explained that drinking blocks folate and that the anemia will come back if the drinking and diet don't change. He heard that. Recheck CBC in about 3 months. Feeling the same, no chest pain.

documents.title: Hypertension Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 53 y/o here to go over blood pressure after finishing the six monthly nurse check-ins. Taking lisinopril every morning, says he hasn't missed. More active since the winter — stairs at work, walks on weekends. Still frustrated: "I'm doing everything and it's still not where you want it."
Nurse visit readings Sep→Feb: 150/92, 148/90, 145/88, 142/86, 140/84, 138/82.
Other problems: obesity, achalasia (stable after dilation), alcohol use disorder, folate deficiency anemia last year (resolved). Alcohol: still daily, didn't want to quantify today.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

O: BP 136/80. BMI 30. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema. Exam otherwise unremarkable.

A/P
1. Essential hypertension: steady improvement with lifestyle changes over six months. Pointed that out to him — 14 points systolic is real progress. Continue lisinopril 20. Home readings, send me a week's worth in a month.
2. T2DM, lipids: labs today. Continue metformin and atorvastatin.
3. AUD: offered resources again.
4. Anemia: CBC with today's labs.
Physical in the fall.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Patient: Darren Upton  DOB 07/10/1971  Arrival 10/02/2025 19:40

HPI: 54 y/o man with prior kidney stone, presenting with two days of left flank pain. Sharp, comes in waves, wraps into the left groin. Nauseated, has not vomited. No fever, no burning with urination, urine looks normal to him.
PMH per patient: diabetes, high blood pressure, gout, achalasia, prior stone.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: T 36.8, HR 88, BP 135/85, SpO2 98%. BMI 32. Uncomfortable, shifting on the stretcher. Left CVA tenderness. Abdomen soft, nontender anteriorly. No rebound.

Results: UA pH 5.0 with uric acid crystals. Serum uric acid 8.6 mg/dL (high). Creatinine and potassium normal. WBC normal.
Renal US: 6 mm stone in the left ureter, no hydronephrosis.

ED course: ketorolac 15 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV with good relief. Tolerating fluids. Repeat vitals normal.

MDM: left ureteral stone, 6 mm, with an acid urine and uric acid crystals — likely a radiolucent uric acid stone. Afebrile, pain controlled, normal renal function, no hydronephrosis: appropriate for outpatient passage trial.

Disposition: discharged 00:30. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily up to 4 weeks, ondansetron ODT as needed, acetaminophen as needed. Strain urine and save any stone. Urology follow-up in 1-2 weeks, sooner for fever, uncontrolled pain or vomiting.

Emergency Medicine

orders.reason: Acute right great toe pain and swelling, history of gout

documents.title: Toe pain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt texted at 6:40 am, called him back. Woke up during the night with the right big toe throbbing; red, swollen, can't stand the sheet on it. No injury. No fever. Remembers the one gout attack years ago, says this is worse.
Likely gout flare. He'd like to see someone who can sort out the gout long-term. Called the rheumatology group; they can see him tomorrow morning. Until then ice, elevate, acetaminophen. Go to urgent care or ED for fever, spreading redness, or if he can't bear weight at all.

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets now, then 1 tablet in 1 hour; then 1 tablet twice daily until the flare resolves

documents.title: Rheumatology consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
RHEUMATOLOGY — NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date of service: 03/26/2026
Patient: Darren Upton, 54 M. Referred urgently by PCP.

HPI: Right great toe pain, redness and swelling for two days. Came on abruptly overnight; throbbing; can barely put a shoe on. On questioning, he has had several smaller episodes over roughly the past two years in the same area that went away within a few days without treatment; he didn't mention them to anyone. Remote first flare years ago. Past history also of a ureteral stone last fall (uric acid crystals in the urine) and an earlier kidney stone.
Other history: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, achalasia treated with dilation, alcohol use disorder.
Medications: lisinopril, metformin, atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with gout and type 2 diabetes; mother with hypertension; paternal uncle with alcohol use disorder.
Social: beer daily, which he acknowledges. Never smoker.

Exam: BMI 32. Afebrile. Right first metatarsophalangeal joint red, warm and exquisitely tender with swelling. No other joints involved. No tophi.

Labs today: serum uric acid 9.2 mg/dL (ref 3.4-7.0), CRP 24 mg/L (ref <5). CBC, creatinine and glucose normal.

Assessment: acute gout flare, right first MTP (podagra), on a background of recurrent flares and uric acid nephrolithiasis.

Plan:
1. Colchicine: 1.2 mg now, 0.6 mg one hour later, then 0.6 mg twice daily until the flare settles.
2. Return in about 6 weeks once quiet to begin urate-lowering therapy with flare prophylaxis.
3. Reduce beer intake — discussed as a major flare trigger.

Rheumatology
